summary: Describes how to connect separate Fibre Channel storage networks over an ordinary IP network by tunneling Fibre Channel frames over TCP. This makes remote storage islands behave like one storage network, relying on IP for the connection between sites.

plainLanguage.summary: FCIP connects Fibre Channel storage networks by carrying their frames over TCP and IP. Devices in the Fibre Channel fabric continue to exchange frames while FCIP manages the link across the IP network.

questions: connecting storage area networks over ip
how are fibre channel frames carried over tcp
subtitle: FCIP carries Fibre Channel frames through TCP connections to join separate storage fabrics across IP.

tldr.problem: Separate Fibre Channel storage networks may need to connect across distances that exceed the normal spacing of Fibre Channel switches.
tldr.mechanism: FCIP encapsulates Fibre Channel frames and sends them over TCP connections between FCIP Entities. An FCIP link joins fabric sections while the IP network carries the traffic.
tldr.outcome: FCIP provides a way to form one Fibre Channel fabric across an IP network and requires IPsec protection. RFC 3821 is updated by RFC 7146.

facts.label: Frame length check
facts.value: Greater than 15 and less than 545 words

today: RFC 3821 is a Proposed Standard, published in July 2004, and is updated by RFC 7146. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Connecting Fibre Channel Sites
sections.content:
Fibre Channel (FC) is a high-speed networking technology used mainly for storage area networks. RFC 3821 defines how to connect separate FC network sections over an IP network, for uses such as remote disk access, tape backup, and live mirroring.

The FC fabric and its devices are meant to remain unaware of the IP transport. The FC side of the connection is covered by Fibre Channel standards; RFC 3821 specifies the TCP/IP requirements for carrying FC frames.
sections.plainLanguage: FCIP links separate Fibre Channel networks through an IP network. Fibre Channel devices continue to exchange frames without handling the IP connection themselves.

sections.title: The FCIP Link and Its Components
sections.content:
An FCIP link connects two portions of one Fibre Channel fabric and contains at least one TCP connection. It may contain more. At each end, an FC Entity interfaces with an FCIP Entity; their interface is specific to the implementation.

An FCIP Entity manages link setup and includes one FCIP Link Endpoint for each link. Each endpoint contains a Data Engine for every TCP connection. The Data Engine encapsulates frames before transmission and removes the encapsulation at the receiving end. Primitive signals, primitive sequences, and Class 1 FC frames are not carried by this protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: An FCIP link joins two parts of a Fibre Channel fabric and uses one or more TCP connections. Data Engines add and remove the framing that lets Fibre Channel frames travel over those connections.

sections.title: Encapsulated Frames and Special Frames
sections.content:
An FCIP frame contains an FC frame inside the FC Frame Encapsulation format. Its Protocol# field is 1. The protocol-specific flags identify an ordinary encapsulated frame or a special frame, and indicate whether an echoed special frame was changed.

The FCIP Special Frame (FSF) appears only as the first bytes sent in each direction on a new TCP connection. It identifies the fabric endpoints and carries connection information, including a random 64-bit connection nonce. The FSF supports link setup; the RFC says it is not a login or parameter-negotiation exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: Each Fibre Channel frame gets an encapsulation header before it enters TCP. A new connection starts with one special frame in each direction to identify the endpoints and share connection details.

sections.title: Opening a TCP Connection
sections.content:
An FCIP Entity must know the peer address and expected identity before it connects. Dynamic discovery, when used, relies on Service Location Protocol version 2. The well-known TCP port is 3225 unless configuration specifies another port.

After TCP accepts the connection, the initiator sends an FSF and waits for an echo. It compares the echoed fields with the ones it sent; a mismatch causes the connection to close. Only after a successful exchange does the entity create or extend the FCIP link and notify the FC Entity. The RFC allows a wait timeout of at least 90 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The two FCIP Entities identify the intended peer before sending Fibre Channel traffic. They exchange and check the opening special frame before using the TCP connection for the link.

sections.title: Protecting the IP Tunnel
sections.content:
An IP network exposes Fibre Channel traffic to monitoring, alteration, injected frames, connection hijacking, impersonation, denial of service, and attacks on discovery. TCP checksums and Fibre Channel checks do not stop a determined attacker who can modify and recalculate them.

FCIP requires IPsec ESP with per-packet origin authentication, integrity, and replay protection; confidentiality is also supported. Implementations MUST support IKE and pre-shared-key authentication, and MUST NOT use manual keying. The default security-association lifetime is one hour and the default replay window is 32 sequence numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: FCIP traffic needs protection because an IP network can expose or alter it. The RFC requires IPsec and IKE so endpoints can authenticate traffic, check its integrity, and prevent replay.

sections.title: Performance and Quality of Service
sections.content:
IP networks do not provide the same predictable latency and throughput as links within a Fibre Channel fabric. An FCIP link can use multiple TCP connections so different traffic can receive different quality-of-service treatment.

The FC Entity supplies each connection's QoS characteristics when it is created, and those characteristics MUST NOT change during the connection. The RFC recommends some form of preferential QoS to reduce latency and packet loss, but does not mandate one particular method.
sections.plainLanguage: Each TCP connection can receive its own quality-of-service settings when it opens. The RFC recommends preferential treatment for FCIP traffic but does not prescribe a specific method.
